encounters.cc: Persistent burning epigastric pain for 9 months, worsening after meals and waking him at night, refractory to standard PPI therapy

lines: Persistent burning epigastric pain for 9 months, worsening after meals and waking him at night, refractory to standard PPI therapy

The patient returns for evaluation approximately four months following his January 2020 gastroenterology encounter for chronic pancreatitis, now presenting with progressive upper gastrointestinal symptoms despite ongoing pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy.
He reports that for the past 9 months he has had burning epigastric pain that worsens after meals and often wakes him at night.
He has been treated by his primary care physician with standard doses of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), which initially gave mild relief, but his symptoms quickly returned.
He has also been prescribed multiple courses of antibiotics for presumed Helicobacter pylori infection, but repeat testing shows no eradication despite appropriate therapy.
The patient describes frequent episodes of nausea and occasional non-bloody vomiting.
He has noticed black, tarry stools on several occasions and attributes this to "ulcers bleeding again." He has lost 15 pounds unintentionally in the past 6 months because eating often triggers pain.
Over-the-counter antacids provide only transient relief.
He is concerned that his symptoms are becoming debilitating and interfering with his job performance.
Despite increasing his PPI dose to twice daily, his ulcers persist, and his pain continues.
- Aspirin 325 mg as needed for headache
His family history is notable for a brother who had hypercalcemia and kidney stones in his 30s.
He has no history of alcohol use disorder or smoking.
The patient works as a software engineer and lives with his partner.
On review of systems, the patient also reports intermittent diarrhea over the past several months.
He notes that the stools are foul-smelling and greasy at times.
He denies hematochezia, but the diarrhea seems to worsen when his ulcer pain flares.
Temperature is 98.4°F, pulse 92/min, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, and respirations 14/min.
On physical examination, the patient appears thin but not acutely ill.
Abdominal exam shows mild tenderness in the epigastrium without rebound or guarding.
No hepatosplenomegaly or palpable masses are noted.
There is no scleral icterus, lymphadenopathy, or skin hyperpigmentation.
Stool studies demonstrate increased fat content, consistent with steatorrhea.
Abdominal CT scan identifies a 2.5-cm enhancing mass in the head of the pancreas.
Biopsies are negative for H. pylori and malignancy.
At his first gastroenterology visit, an upper endoscopy reveals multiple duodenal ulcers, including one in the distal duodenum.
The gastric folds appear thickened, and the stomach contains copious amounts of acid.
The patient is admitted for further management.

lines: Vomiting blood and dark stools with abdominal fullness and nausea
The patient with chronic pancreatitis, prior upper GI bleeding, and malnutrition presents to the ICU.
The patient reports that over the past 2 days he has had increasing episodes of nausea, a feeling of abdominal fullness, and dark stools.
Since that time, he has noticed intermittent upper abdominal discomfort, early satiety, and occasional bloating after meals.
- NSAID-induced gastropathy or upper gastrointestinal bleeding (diagnosed 2023-07-15)
